title: Au, aux, du, des
description: Join à and de with le and les: au cinéma, aux cartes, la fin du film.

guide.summary: À and de swallow the articles le and les: au, aux, du, des. Learn the four forms that follow each preposition and you can say where you are going, where you come from and what belongs to whom.

sections.title: Which form after à?
sections.text: À plus le or les is never written as two words. À la and à l’ are left exactly as they are.
steps: Find the noun after the blank and the article it takes: le, la, l’ or les.
Read that row: only le and les merge with à.
A singular noun starting with a vowel or a silent h always takes the l’ row, whatever its gender.

examples.en: I am going to the market.
She is talking to the neighbours.

watch: À always carries a grave accent; a with no accent is the verb avoir (he has).
Aux stays aux before a vowel, because les never shortens: aux élèves, aux États-Unis.

sections.title: Which form after de?
sections.text: De behaves exactly like à: it merges with le and les, and leaves la and l’ alone.
steps: Decide which article the noun takes: le, la, l’ or les.
Merge only with le and les; the other two rows keep their two words.
Check gender before you merge: a -e ending is not a promise of feminine (le musée).

examples.en: He is coming back from the office.
She is coming out of the bakery.

watch: Des here means “of the”, not “some”: le sac des étudiants.
De le and de les are never correct, in any sentence.

sections.title: Before a vowel or a silent h
sections.text: Le and la shorten to l’ in front of a vowel sound, so the merged singular forms cannot appear there.
steps: Say the noun out loud: does it start with a vowel sound?
If it does and it is singular, take the l’ forms for both prepositions.
If it is plural, keep the plural contractions, vowel or no vowel.

examples.en: We are coming back from the university.

watch: Never au hôtel or du université: the article shortens first.
A few h words behave like consonants and keep the merged form: jouer au hockey.

sections.title: Where the contraction happens
sections.text: The merge happens wherever à or de meets an article: after verbs, after place words, and in phrases of belonging.

rows: aller à, être à, penser à, téléphoner à, donner à
parler de, venir de, revenir de, sortir de, avoir peur de
près de, loin de, à côté de, en face de
la fin du film, le sac des étudiants, la maison des voisins

steps: Spot the word that demands à or de: the verb or the place word.
Add the noun with its own article.
Apply the contraction table to that pair.

examples.fr: La pharmacie est à côté du parc.
examples.en: The chemist’s is next to the park.

watch: English says “the children’s room”; French says the room of the children: la chambre des enfants.
Keep the article: près de musée and loin de parc are incomplete.

sections.title: What never merges
sections.text: Only the articles le and les merge. The identical-looking words placed before a verb are object pronouns and stay apart.

rows: La never merges: à la plage, près de la gare.
L’ never merges: à l’école, de l’hôtel.
There they are object pronouns, not articles: je commence à le lire.

steps: Look at what follows le or les: a noun or a verb?
A noun means it is an article, so merge it with the preposition.
A verb means it is an object pronoun, so leave the two words apart.

examples.en: I am starting to read it.
He is trying to sell them.

watch: À la and de la are two words in every sentence; nothing ever shortens them.

sections.title: Jouer à or jouer de?
sections.text: Jouer picks its preposition from what is being played.

rows: jouer au tennis, aux cartes, au foot
jouer du piano, de la guitare, du violon

steps: Name what is played: a sport or game, or a musical instrument?
Sports and games take à; instruments take de.
Then merge that preposition with the noun’s article as usual.
watch: Jouer du basket and jouer au piano are both wrong: check the category first.
Gender and number still count: la guitare keeps its two words, les cartes takes the plural form.

steps: Check the noun: masculine singular, starting with a consonant?
Then à and its article cannot stay as two words: take the merged form from the table.
Feminine nouns and vowel-sound nouns belong to another row.
Ask whether the noun is plural: does it take les?
À plus a plural article always fuses into one word; find that row.
A vowel at the start of the noun changes nothing for plurals.
Decide the gender, then listen to the first sound of the noun.
Feminine plus a consonant keeps the preposition and the article apart.
Any singular noun starting with a vowel or a silent h takes the shortened article, masculine or feminine.
Keep the grave accent on the preposition.
Find the verb or place word that demands de.
Check the noun: masculine singular with a consonant start?
Then de and its article merge into the single form of the table.
Ask whether the noun is plural, including in belonging phrases (the X of the Y).
De plus a plural article always fuses into one word.
Check the noun keeps its plural -s.
Decide the gender, then listen to the first sound of the noun.
Feminine plus a consonant leaves the two words untouched.
A vowel or a silent h shortens the article instead of merging it.
Name what is played: sport or game, or musical instrument?
Sports and games go with à, instruments with de.
Then apply the contraction for the noun’s gender and number.

exercises.feedback: À and the article le never stay side by side.
exercises.explanation: À + le always contracts to au: je vais au cinéma.

mistakes.why: French never leaves à and the article le side by side; the two words fuse into a single one.
À la introduces a feminine noun, and cinéma is masculine: le cinéma.

exercises.source: Mon père est ____ bureau jusqu’à six heures.
exercises.hint: Bureau is masculine and begins with a consonant.
exercises.feedback: À + le contracts.
exercises.explanation: Le bureau is masculine, so à + le becomes au: être au bureau.

mistakes.why: À followed by the article le is always written as one word, never as two.
The shortened article l’ appears only before a vowel or a silent h, and bureau starts with the consonant b.

exercises.instruction: Write au, à la, à l’ or aux.
exercises.feedback: À + le contracts into one word.
exercises.explanation: Le marché is masculine, so à + le becomes au: aller au marché.

mistakes.why: À and le never survive as two separate words in front of a noun.
That is the feminine form, but marché is masculine: le marché.
That is the plural form. Here there is one market, so a singular form is needed.
L’ replaces le or la only before a vowel or a silent h; marché begins with m.

exercises.instruction: Replace la plage with le parc.
exercises.source: Les enfants vont à la plage.
exercises.hint: À la does not change, but à + le does.
exercises.feedback: With a masculine noun, à and le merge.
exercises.explanation: Le parc is masculine, so à + le becomes au: ils vont au parc.

answers: Les enfants vont à le parc.
mistakes.why: You kept the preposition and the article apart; in front of a masculine noun they must be written as one word.

answers: Les enfants vont à la parc.
mistakes.why: Parc is masculine (le parc), so the feminine article la does not fit.
That plural form needs a plural noun; here there is one park.

exercises.source: I am going to the restaurant.
exercises.hint: Restaurant is masculine. Use aller à.
exercises.feedback: To the with a masculine noun is one word.
exercises.explanation: Le restaurant is masculine, so to the restaurant is au restaurant.

mistakes.why: À plus the article le is never written as two words.
Restaurant is masculine: le restaurant, not la restaurant.
The article disappeared. French keeps it, and it then fuses with the preposition.

exercises.source: Tu penses à le match de demain ?
answers: Tu penses au match de demain ?
exercises.feedback: À + the article le is never written as two words.
exercises.explanation: À + le always contracts to au: penser au match.

answers: Tu penses à le match de demain ?
mistakes.why: That is the sentence untouched: penser à plus le match cannot stay in two words.

answers: Tu penses à la match de demain ?
mistakes.why: Match is masculine (le match), so the feminine article is wrong here too.

answers: Tu penses aux match de demain ?
mistakes.why: The plural contraction needs a plural noun, and there is one match.

exercises.instruction: Build the French sentence. Leave any extra tiles unused.
exercises.source: He is going to the stadium.
exercises.hint: Stade is masculine. Two tiles stay unused.
exercises.feedback: À + le becomes one word.
exercises.explanation: Le stade is masculine, so à + le becomes au: il va au stade.

mistakes.why: Those two small tiles are the trap: à and le cannot stand next to each other, which is why the merged tile is in the set.
The article is missing: stade takes le, and le then fuses with the preposition.

exercises.feedback: À + les contracts too.
exercises.explanation: À + les always contracts to aux: penser aux vacances.

mistakes.why: À and the plural article are never written apart; they always fuse into one word.
Au is the masculine singular form. Vacances is plural (les vacances), so it needs the plural contraction.

exercises.hint: Élèves is plural, even though it begins with a vowel.
exercises.feedback: À + les contracts, before a vowel as well.
exercises.explanation: À + les becomes aux for all plurals: parler aux élèves.

mistakes.why: The preposition and the plural article always merge into one word.
L’ replaces le or la for one singular noun. Élèves is plural, and les never shortens before a vowel.

exercises.feedback: Au is only for a masculine singular noun.
exercises.explanation: Les parents is plural, so à + les becomes aux: téléphoner aux parents.

mistakes.why: Au is the masculine singular form, and les parents is plural.
The preposition and les never stay as two words.
That is the feminine singular form, and parents is plural.

exercises.source: Il donne un cadeau à l’enfant.
answers: Il donne un cadeau aux enfants.
exercises.hint: À l’ does not change, but à + les does.
exercises.feedback: With a plural noun, à and les merge.
exercises.explanation: À + les becomes aux: il donne un cadeau aux enfants.

answers: Il donne un cadeau à les enfants.
mistakes.why: You made the noun plural but left the preposition and the article apart; they must fuse.

answers: Il donne un cadeau à l’enfants.
mistakes.why: L’ is a singular article; it cannot introduce a plural noun.

answers: Il donne un cadeau aux enfant.
mistakes.why: The article is plural but the noun is not: after les, enfant takes its -s.

exercises.source: Je donne du pain à les oiseaux.
answers: Je donne du pain aux oiseaux.
exercises.feedback: À + the article les is never written as two words.
exercises.explanation: À + les always contracts to aux: aux oiseaux.

answers: Je donne du pain à les oiseaux.
mistakes.why: Nothing was changed: à and les cannot stay side by side.

answers: Je donne du pain au oiseaux.
mistakes.why: Au is masculine singular, oiseaux is plural, and au never stands before a vowel either.

answers: Je donne du pain à l’oiseaux.
mistakes.why: L’ introduces one singular noun; les oiseaux is plural.

exercises.source: They (ils) live in the United States.
exercises.hint: The country name is les États-Unis, which is plural.
exercises.feedback: In the United States uses à + les.
exercises.explanation: Les États-Unis is plural, so à + les becomes aux: ils habitent aux États-Unis.

mistakes.why: The preposition and les always merge; they cannot be written apart.
Au is the masculine singular form, and the country is les États-Unis, a plural name.
En is used with feminine country names (en France). A plural country name keeps its article after the preposition.

exercises.feedback: Au is not used before a vowel.
exercises.explanation: Before a vowel, use à l’, never au: à l’école.

mistakes.why: Au is the masculine merged form and never stands before a vowel sound; école begins with é.
École is feminine, but in front of a vowel the article la loses its own vowel and takes an apostrophe.

exercises.feedback: À la never contracts.
exercises.explanation: La montagne is feminine, and à la stays as two words: à la montagne.

mistakes.why: Au is the masculine merged form; montagne is feminine: la montagne.
À and le are never written apart, and montagne is feminine anyway, so le is wrong twice over.

exercises.instruction: Write au, à la or à l’.
exercises.hint: The h in hôpital is silent.
exercises.feedback: Hôpital sounds as if it begins with a vowel.
exercises.explanation: Before a silent h, use à l’, not au: à l’hôpital.

mistakes.why: Au never stands in front of a vowel sound, and the h of hôpital is silent.
Hôpital is masculine, and before a silent h the article shortens with an apostrophe anyway.
A without an accent is the verb avoir (he has). The preposition always carries its grave accent.

exercises.instruction: Write au, à la or à l’.
exercises.feedback: With a feminine noun, à and la stay apart. Check the accent.
exercises.explanation: La piscine is feminine, so à la does not change: aller à la piscine. À has a grave accent.

mistakes.why: Au is the masculine merged form; piscine is feminine: la piscine.
A with no accent is the verb avoir (he has). The preposition needs its grave accent.
The apostrophe form appears only before a vowel or a silent h, and piscine begins with p.

exercises.source: Je vais au hôtel ce soir.
answers: Je vais à l’hôtel ce soir.
spellingAnswers: Je vais à l’hotel ce soir.
exercises.hint: The h in hôtel is silent.
exercises.feedback: Au is not used before a vowel sound.
exercises.explanation: Hôtel has a silent h, so à + le becomes à l’, not au: à l’hôtel.

answers: Je vais au hôtel ce soir.
mistakes.why: The sentence is unchanged: au cannot stand before the silent h of hôtel.

answers: Je vais à le hôtel ce soir.
mistakes.why: You split the word in two, but before a silent h the article itself must shorten.

answers: Je vais à la hôtel ce soir.
mistakes.why: Hôtel is masculine, and the article shortens before its silent h.

exercises.hint: Plage is feminine. Use être à.
exercises.feedback: With a feminine noun, the preposition does not merge. Check the accent on the preposition.
exercises.explanation: La plage is feminine, so at the beach is à la plage. À needs its grave accent.

mistakes.why: Au is the masculine merged form; plage is feminine: la plage.
The preposition lost its accent: a alone is the verb avoir (he has).
Le is masculine and never stands as a separate word after this preposition; plage is feminine.

exercises.source: She is going to the airport.
exercises.hint: Aéroport begins with a vowel. One tile stays unused.
exercises.feedback: Au is not used before a vowel.
exercises.explanation: Before a vowel, use à l’: elle va à l’aéroport.

mistakes.why: The merged tile cannot be used before a vowel; that is why the two short tiles are in the set.
The article is missing: aéroport needs one, shortened before its vowel.

exercises.feedback: De and the article le never stay side by side.
exercises.explanation: De + le always contracts to du: la fin du film.

mistakes.why: De and the article le are never written as two separate words.
That is the plural form, but film here is one singular noun.

exercises.source: La pharmacie est à côté ____ parc.
exercises.feedback: Parc is masculine; de + le contracts.
exercises.explanation: À côté de + le parc becomes à côté du parc.

mistakes.why: De plus le always fuses into one word.
That is the feminine form; parc is masculine: le parc.

exercises.instruction: Write du, de la, de l’ or des.
exercises.source: Il parle ____ match avec ses amis.
exercises.feedback: Match is masculine singular.
exercises.explanation: De + le contracts to du: parler du match.

mistakes.why: De and le are never written apart.
Match is masculine (le match), so the feminine form does not fit.
That is the plural form, and there is one match here.
L’ appears only before a vowel or a silent h; match starts with m.

exercises.instruction: Replace la gare with le musée.
exercises.source: Nous habitons près de la gare.
exercises.hint: De la does not change, but de + le does.
exercises.feedback: With a masculine noun, de and le merge.
exercises.explanation: Le musée is masculine, so près de + le becomes près du musée.

answers: Nous habitons près de le musée.
mistakes.why: You kept de and le apart; with a masculine noun they must be written as one word.

answers: Nous habitons près de la musée.
mistakes.why: Musée is masculine (le musée) in spite of its ending.
The article disappeared: près de needs the noun with its article, and the two then fuse.

exercises.source: The school is far from the park.
exercises.feedback: Far from the with a masculine noun is one word.
exercises.explanation: Le parc is masculine, so loin de + le becomes loin du parc.

answers: L’école est loin de le parc.
mistakes.why: De plus le is never written in two words.

answers: L’école est loin de la parc.
mistakes.why: Parc is masculine: le parc.
That is the plural form, but there is only one park here.

exercises.feedback: De + the article le is never written as two words.
exercises.explanation: De + le always contracts to du: elle revient du supermarché.

mistakes.why: Nothing changed: de and le cannot stand side by side.
Supermarché is masculine: le supermarché.
That is the plural form and the noun here is singular.

exercises.instruction: Build the French sentence. Leave any extra tiles unused.
exercises.source: I am coming back from the office.
exercises.hint: Bureau is masculine. Two tiles stay unused.
exercises.feedback: De + le becomes one word.
exercises.explanation: Le bureau is masculine, so de + le becomes du: je reviens du bureau.

mistakes.why: Those two tiles are the trap; de and le must give way to the single merged tile.
The article is missing: revenir de plus le bureau gives one merged word.

exercises.feedback: De and the article les never stay side by side.
exercises.explanation: De + les always contracts to des: le livre des enfants.

mistakes.why: De and the plural article never stay apart; they fuse into one word.
Du is the masculine singular form, and enfants is plural: les enfants.

exercises.feedback: Vacances is plural.
exercises.explanation: De + les contracts to des: parler des vacances.

mistakes.why: De plus les is always written as a single word.
That is the feminine singular form; vacances is plural.

exercises.source: La maison ____ voisins est très grande.
exercises.feedback: Du is only for a masculine singular noun.
exercises.explanation: The house of the neighbours: de + les voisins becomes des voisins.

mistakes.why: Du is for a masculine singular noun, but voisins is plural.
De and les are never written as two words.
That is the feminine singular form, and the noun here is plural.

exercises.hint: De l’ does not change, but de + les does.
exercises.feedback: With a plural noun, de and les merge.
exercises.explanation: De + les becomes des: le sac des étudiants.

answers: C’est le sac de les étudiants.
mistakes.why: You made the noun plural but left the preposition and the article apart; they must fuse.
Du is masculine singular and never stands before a vowel; étudiants is plural.
L’ belongs to one singular noun; once the noun is plural it needs the plural article.

exercises.feedback: De + the article les is never written as two words.
exercises.explanation: De + les always contracts to des: j’ai peur des chiens.

mistakes.why: The sentence is unchanged: de and les cannot stay side by side.
Du is masculine singular, but chiens is plural.
The article dropped out: avoir peur de plus les chiens keeps the article, merged with de.

answers: La chambre des enfants est bleue.
exercises.hint: French says the room of the children.
exercises.feedback: Of the with a plural noun is one word.
exercises.explanation: The children’s room is la chambre de + les enfants, which becomes des enfants.

answers: La chambre de les enfants est bleue.
mistakes.why: De and les never stay as two words.

answers: La chambre du enfants est bleue.
mistakes.why: Du is masculine singular and cannot precede a vowel; enfants is plural.
That is English word order. French says the room of the children, with the owner after the noun.

exercises.source: Elle sort ____ boulangerie avec du pain.
exercises.feedback: De la never contracts.
exercises.explanation: La boulangerie is feminine, so de la stays: sortir de la boulangerie.

mistakes.why: Du is the masculine merged form; boulangerie is feminine: la boulangerie.
De and le are never written apart, and the noun here is feminine anyway.

exercises.feedback: Du is not used before a vowel.
exercises.explanation: Before a vowel, use de l’: rentrer de l’école.

mistakes.why: Du never stands before a vowel sound, and école begins with é.
École is feminine, but before a vowel the article la loses its vowel and takes an apostrophe.

exercises.instruction: Write du, de la or de l’.
exercises.source: Le parking est en face ____ hôtel.
exercises.hint: The h in hôtel is silent.
exercises.feedback: Du is not used before a vowel sound.
exercises.explanation: Hôtel has a silent h, so en face de + l’hôtel gives de l’hôtel.

mistakes.why: Du cannot stand before a vowel sound, and the h of hôtel is silent.
Hôtel is masculine, and before its silent h the article shortens with an apostrophe.
De and le are never written as two words, and before a silent h the article shortens anyway.

exercises.source: The bank is opposite the train station.
answers: La banque est en face de la gare.
exercises.hint: Opposite is en face de. Gare is feminine.
exercises.feedback: With a feminine noun, de and la stay apart.
exercises.explanation: La gare is feminine, so de la does not change: en face de la gare.

answers: La banque est en face du gare.
mistakes.why: Du is the masculine merged form; gare is feminine: la gare.

answers: La banque est en face de le gare.
mistakes.why: De and le never stay apart, and gare is feminine.

answers: La banque est en face des gare.
mistakes.why: That is the plural form; there is one station here.

exercises.feedback: Du is not used before a vowel.
exercises.explanation: Before a vowel, use de l’: il vient de l’université.

mistakes.why: Unchanged: du cannot stand before a vowel sound.
The article cannot keep its vowel in front of université; it shortens with an apostrophe.
Université is feminine, and before a vowel the article shortens anyway.

exercises.instruction: Replace le café with la mairie.
exercises.source: Le bus s’arrête près du café.
answers: Le bus s’arrête près de la mairie.
exercises.feedback: With a feminine noun, de and la do not merge.
exercises.explanation: La mairie is feminine, so près de la stays in two words: près de la mairie.

answers: Le bus s’arrête près du mairie.
mistakes.why: Du is the masculine merged form; mairie is feminine: la mairie.

answers: Le bus s’arrête près de le mairie.
mistakes.why: De and le are never written apart, and mairie is feminine.

answers: Le bus s’arrête près de mairie.
mistakes.why: The article is missing: près de needs the noun with its article.

exercises.feedback: For sports and games, jouer takes à.
exercises.explanation: Jouer à is for sports, and tennis is masculine: jouer au tennis.

mistakes.why: Both come from jouer de, which introduces a musical instrument. Tennis is a sport, so jouer needs the other preposition.

exercises.feedback: For instruments, jouer takes de.
exercises.explanation: Jouer de is for instruments, and piano is masculine: jouer du piano.

mistakes.why: Au comes from jouer à, which covers sports and games; the piano is an instrument.
À and le are never written apart, and instruments do not take à in the first place.

exercises.hint: Guitare is an instrument and is feminine.

exercises.explanation: Jouer de is for instruments, and guitare is feminine, so de la stays: jouer de la guitare.

mistakes.why: Jouer à is for sports and games; a guitar is an instrument, so the other preposition is needed.
That is the masculine instrument form, but guitare is feminine: la guitare.

exercises.instruction: Write au, aux, du or de la.
exercises.hint: Cards are a game, and cartes is plural.
exercises.feedback: Games take à with jouer.
exercises.explanation: Jouer à is for games, and cartes is plural: jouer aux cartes.

mistakes.why: Both come from jouer de, which is for musical instruments. Cards are a game, so jouer takes à here.
Au is the masculine singular form, and cartes is plural: les cartes.
À and les are never written as two words.

exercises.instruction: Write au, aux, du or de la.
exercises.source: Elle joue ____ violon depuis dix ans.
exercises.feedback: Instruments take de with jouer.
exercises.explanation: Jouer de is for instruments, and violon is masculine: jouer du violon.

mistakes.why: Au comes from jouer à, for sports and games; a violin is an instrument.
Violon is masculine (le violon), so the feminine article is wrong.
That is the plural form of jouer à: it points at a game, and a violin is one instrument.
De and le are never written as two words.

exercises.feedback: Sports take à with jouer.
exercises.explanation: Jouer à is for sports, and football is masculine: ils jouent au football.

mistakes.why: That is the instrument form of jouer; football is a sport.
English says “play football”, but jouer needs a preposition before the sport, not the bare article.
The preposition is the right one, but à and le are never written as two words.

exercises.feedback: Instruments take de with jouer.
exercises.explanation: Jouer de is for instruments: je joue du piano.

mistakes.why: Au comes from jouer à, which covers sports and games; the piano is an instrument.
Jouer needs a preposition before an instrument, not just the article.
The preposition is right, but de and le are never written apart.

exercises.source: Je joue du basket le samedi.
answers: Je joue au basket le samedi.
exercises.hint: Basket is a sport, not an instrument.
exercises.feedback: Sports and instruments take different prepositions.
exercises.explanation: Jouer à is for sports: je joue au basket.

answers: Je joue du basket le samedi.
mistakes.why: The sentence is untouched: that form belongs to jouer de, which is for instruments, and basket is a sport.

answers: Je joue de la basket le samedi.
mistakes.why: This is still jouer de, the instrument construction, and basket is a sport.

answers: Je joue à le basket le samedi.
mistakes.why: The preposition is right now, but à and le are never written as two words.

exercises.feedback: Instruments take de with jouer.
exercises.explanation: Jouer de is for instruments, and guitare is feminine: jouer de la guitare.

mistakes.why: That tile is the trap: à goes with sports and games, and a guitar is an instrument.
English drops the words before the instrument, French does not: jouer needs its preposition and the article.
